Whiskey Bar in Sapporo’s Susukino | Rock Bar FxxK Up

Try Yoichi and Akkeshi from Hokkaido alongside a pour of Yamazaki, then tell us what rock song you want to hear. We’re a four-minute walk from Susukino Station. Browse all 173 whiskies and their prices below.

Drink it how you like it

Don’t let anyone tell you there’s only one right way to drink whiskey. We might suggest a way to try it, or tell you how we like it, but you’re the one drinking it. You decide what you enjoy.

Selection and availability can change.

These sections group whiskies by Japanese producer. Some bottles are world blends made with whisky from Japan and other countries, so a Japanese brand name doesn’t always mean the whisky was made entirely in Japan.

Japanese Whisky — Nikka

Nikka is a good place to compare two different styles: Yoichi brings peat smoke and weight, while Miyagikyo leans more toward fruit and malt. There’s plenty beyond those single malts too, including Taketsuru, Coffey whiskies and blends such as From The Barrel.

Japanese Whisky — Suntory

Suntory gives you several directions to go. Yamazaki has a rich, layered style; Hakushu brings fresh herbal notes and gentle smoke; Chita is a lighter grain whisky. Hibiki and Toki show what happens when different distillery styles come together in a blend.

Japanese Whisky — Ichiro’s Malt

There’s a lot to compare in Ichiro Akuto’s range. Mizunara Wood Reserve uses Japanese oak, while Wine Wood Reserve uses wine casks. You’ll also find Malt & Grain world blends and different Double Distilleries releases.

Japanese Whisky — Other

Japan’s whisky scene goes well beyond Nikka and Suntory. This section takes in Sakurao Sherry Cask, Fuji and Tsunuki single malts, Mars blends and Okinawa’s rice-based Island Blue. There’s a lot of variety here, including both Japanese whisky and world blends.

Japanese Whisky — Akkeshi

Akkeshi makes whisky on Hokkaido’s east coast, with peat smoke playing a big part in its style. The seasonal names come from the Twenty-Four Solar Terms series; each release has its own balance of smoke, fruit and sweetness.

Bourbon

Scotch — Islay

If you like smoky whisky, start here. Islay is known for peat, and Port Charlotte gives you plenty of it. Bruichladdich Classic Laddie takes a different route: it’s unpeated, with more of a fruity, floral style.

Scotch — Blended

This section includes two kinds of blend. Blended Scotch combines malt and grain whisky; blended malt brings together single malts from different distilleries. Johnnie Walker Green Label, for example, is a blended malt. It’s worth checking the label rather than assuming all blends are the same.

Scotch — Campbeltown

Campbeltown has a small footprint and a lot of variety, from malty sweetness to coastal notes and smoke. Springbank, Kilkerran and Glen Scotia show different sides of it; Longrow is worth a look if you want more peat.

Tennessee Whiskey

Jack Daniel’s is filtered through sugar-maple charcoal before aging. Gentleman Jack gets a second charcoal mellowing afterward. If you already know Jack, this is an easy comparison, with caramel and vanilla running through both.

  • Jack Daniels¥800
  • Gentleman Jack¥900

Iowa Whiskey

Slipknot No. 9 brings the band and Iowa’s Cedar Ridge distillery together. It blends straight bourbon with straight rye, giving you American whiskey with both sweetness and spice.

  • Slipknot No. 9¥1,200

Canadian Whisky

Canadian Club 12 is a straightforward place to start, with vanilla, honey and a little spice. Canadian whisky covers a wide range, so go by the bottle rather than expecting everything here to taste alike.

  • Canadian Club 12 Year¥800
  • Banff¥1,500
  • Coureur des Bois¥1,500

Indian Whisky

Paul John Brilliance is an unpeated single malt from Goa. Think honey, vanilla and a little cocoa and spice. It’s worth a look if you usually enjoy sweeter malt whiskies and want to try something from India.

  • Paul John Brilliance¥1,200

Welsh Whisky

Penderyn Madeira starts in bourbon barrels before finishing in Madeira wine casks. The result is a fruity Welsh single malt with toffee and raisin notes and a drier finish. Try this section if you’re curious about wine-cask finishes.

  • Penderyn Madeira¥1,300

Israeli Whisky

M&H Classic comes from Tel Aviv, with bourbon and specially treated red-wine casks in the mix. Vanilla, honey and a little pepper make it a good starting point if you haven’t tried Israeli single malt before.

  • M&H Classic¥1,100

Danish Whisky

Thornæs makes single malt in Kagerup, Denmark. The Sherry Oloroso listing is one for anyone curious about sherry-cask whisky and what a smaller Danish producer is doing.

  • Thornaes Sherry Oloroso15ml ¥1,000 / 30ml ¥2,000
